chapter.name: The World of Metals and Non-metals

questions.q: A scrap dealer hammers five unlabelled samples. V and X spread into flat plates, W and Z crumble into pieces, and Y neither flattens nor crumbles. He knows the five are copper, iron, coal, sulfur and wood. Which sample is the wood?
questions.a: Y: wood is neither malleable nor brittle, so it is the one that stays whole and unflattened. V and X flatten (metals) and W and Z break (coal, sulfur).
o: Y, because it neither flattens nor breaks
W, because it crumbles when it is struck
Z, because it breaks without any flattening
V, because it flattens without ever breaking

questions.q: A student tells her friend, 'A material that does not break when hammered must be malleable.' Which single observation would show her that she is wrong?
questions.a: A block of wood: it does not break, but it also does not flatten into a sheet, so it is neither malleable nor brittle.
o: A wooden block stays whole yet does not flatten
A lump of coal crumbles into small pieces
An iron nail becomes flat when it is beaten
A copper piece spreads into a thin plate

questions.q: Four students write conclusions from their hammering notes. Which conclusion is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: A material that is hammered and does not break need not be malleable (wood). The other three conclusions match the chapter.
o: Whatever stays whole under the hammer is malleable
A soft solid cut by a knife may still be a metal
A liquid at room temperature can still be a metal
A material that breaks into pieces is not malleable

questions.q: Ravi hammers a shiny 5 cm strip of an unknown material on an anvil. It spreads into a thin sheet without cracking. Then he finds he cannot cut it with a knife. What should he note in his table?
questions.a: It is lustrous, hard and malleable, like copper or aluminium. Sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut, and brittle sulfur and coal would break.
o: Probably a metal such as aluminium: hard and malleable
Probably a soft metal such as sodium, since it flattened
Probably a non-metal such as sulfur, since it is hard
Probably wood, since it did not break when hammered

questions.q: A science club has to decide which sample could NOT be safely called a non-metal on the evidence given. Which one is it?
questions.a: A shiny solid that a knife cuts easily: sodium and potassium are metals soft enough to be cut, so softness does not make a material a non-metal.
o: A shiny solid that a knife cuts easily
A dull lump that crumbles when struck
A dull block that neither flattens nor breaks
A dull powder that does not conduct

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mercury is classified as a metal.
Reason (R): Mercury is used inside thermometers.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but classification as a metal does not come from its use in thermometers; the chapter calls it a metal that is liquid at room temperature. So the reason does not explain the assertion.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about metals in early India.
Statement 1: The Harappans used copper and gold to make objects from utensils to jewellery.
Statement 2: Evidence of iron is hardly found at Harappan sites because iron was too weak to make tools.
Statement 3: Once iron was in common use, iron ploughs were much superior to earlier ones because of iron's strength.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are true. 2 is false: the chapter says iron was not used in day-to-day life for a long time, not that it was weak; its strength is why iron ploughs were superior.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each hammering result in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. A pea-sized lump crumbles into pieces. 2. A shiny strip spreads into a thin sheet. 3. A block stays whole and unflattened. 4. A silvery material in a thermometer is liquid at room temperature.
Column II: a. A malleable metal. b. A brittle material. c. Neither malleable nor brittle. d. A metal in a liquid state.
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: 1-b (brittle), 2-a (malleable metal), 3-c (neither), 4-d (mercury, a liquid metal).

questions.q: A carpenter's block hammered on an anvil neither flattens nor breaks into pieces, so it is neither malleable nor ___.
questions.a: brittle

questions.q:
(a) A sweet shop uses silver foil on its sweets and aluminium foil to pack its tiffins. Name the property both foils show.
(b) Explain why a foil of the same thinness cannot be made from coal.
questions.a: (a) Malleability. (b) Coal is brittle: it breaks into pieces when beaten instead of spreading into a sheet.
s: (a) malleability
(b) coal breaks into pieces instead of flattening

questions.q:
(a) Name the two observations that together separate a piece of copper from a lump of coal in Table 4.1.
(b) A shiny solid is easily cut with a knife. Why can you not declare it a non-metal?
questions.a: (a) Copper is lustrous and hard; coal is non-lustrous and not as hard (and it also breaks when hammered). (b) Sodium and potassium are metals that are soft enough to be cut with a knife.
s: (a) copper lustrous and hard versus coal non-lustrous and softer
(b) soft metals such as sodium and potassium exist

questions.q:
(a) What does the chapter say about the evidence of iron among the Harappans?
(b) A student concludes, 'So the Harappans were less skilled with metals.' Give one fact from the chapter that weakens this conclusion.
questions.a: (a) Hardly any evidence of iron is found, because it took a long time before iron was used in day-to-day activities. (b) They skilfully used copper and gold for objects from utensils to jewellery, so the absence of iron reflects when iron came into use, not a lack of skill.
s: (a) hardly any evidence; iron entered day-to-day use late
(b) copper and gold worked into utensils and jewellery

questions.q:
(a) Of copper, mercury, sulfur and wood, which one cannot be given a hammering test at all, and why?
(b) For the other three, say which flattens and what the remaining two do.
questions.a: (a) Mercury: it is a liquid at room temperature, so it cannot be beaten into a sheet. (b) Copper flattens; sulfur breaks into pieces; wood neither flattens nor breaks.
s: (a) mercury, liquid at room temperature
(b) copper flattens, sulfur breaks, wood does neither

questions.q: Nitin says, 'Gold and silver are the most malleable metals, so gold and silver are the only metals that can be made into thin sheets.' Is he right?
questions.a: Partly. Gold and silver are indeed the most malleable. But he is wrong about 'only': copper, aluminium and the iron nail also become flat on beating (Activity 4.1), and aluminium foil is used to wrap food.
s: verdict: partly right
gold and silver are the most malleable
copper, aluminium and iron also flatten, so 'only' is wrong

questions.q: Asha writes, 'A metal is a material that does not break when hammered.' Do you agree?
questions.a: No. Wood does not break when hammered either, yet it is not a metal. A metal flattens into a sheet (malleable); wood neither flattens nor breaks, and coal and sulfur break.
s: verdict: no
wood does not break but is not a metal
metals flatten, which is a different behaviour from not breaking

questions.q: Using only a hammer and a knife, design a test on three unlabelled samples that would help you tell a metal such as iron, a brittle non-metal such as sulfur and a piece of wood apart. Say what you expect to see for each.
questions.a: Hammer each: iron flattens into a sheet; sulfur breaks into pieces; wood neither flattens nor breaks. A knife test must not be used alone, because soft metals such as sodium can be cut too.
s: iron flattens under the hammer
sulfur breaks and wood does neither
a knife test alone would mislead because some metals are soft

questions.q: Sheela proposes a one-line rule for her class chart: 'Hammer it. If it flattens, it is a metal; if not, it is a non-metal.' Test her rule against the chapter's materials. Say which materials it classifies correctly, which material it cannot test at all, what other fact shows one more flaw in the usual picture of metals, and suggest a better rule.
questions.a: Copper, aluminium and iron flatten (metals, correct). Coal and sulfur break and wood does neither, so they are correctly non-metals. Mercury is a liquid, so it cannot be hammered, yet it is a metal. Sodium and potassium are metals soft enough to cut with a knife, so a hardness idea would fail. A better rule uses several properties (lustre, hardness, malleability) with the word 'generally'.
s: flattening materials copper, aluminium and iron are metals
coal, sulfur and wood correctly non-metals
mercury cannot be hammered at all
sodium and potassium are soft metals
better rule uses several properties and 'generally'

questions.q: A student's project says: 'The Harappans used copper and gold but hardly any iron, so they were less skilled than the people who later used iron.' Evaluate this statement. Say what the chapter's evidence shows, what it does not show, why iron ploughs later mattered, and what question the chapter leaves open.
questions.a: The chapter shows the Harappans made utensils and jewellery from copper and gold, and that iron was hardly used because it took a long time before it entered day-to-day use. This is about timing, not skill, so the conclusion is not supported. Once iron was in use, its strength made ploughs much superior. The chapter leaves open why copper is generally thought to have been discovered before iron, so no claim about why is given.
s: copper and gold objects shown by the chapter
iron's late day-to-day use is about timing, not skill
strength made iron ploughs much superior
the chapter leaves open why copper came before iron
overall judgement: conclusion unsupported

questions.q: A student's record sheet has only two columns for the hammer test: 'flattens' and 'breaks'. Explain why wood causes trouble, what third entry the sheet needs, and what that shows about the words malleable and brittle.
questions.a: Wood neither flattens nor breaks, so it fits neither column. The sheet needs a third entry, 'neither'. So 'not malleable' does not mean 'brittle': a material can be neither malleable nor brittle.
s: wood fits neither column
third entry: neither flattens nor breaks
not malleable does not mean brittle

questions.q:
At a Jaipur science fair, three unlabelled exhibits are shown. Exhibit 1: a silvery liquid sealed in a glass tube for a thermometer. Exhibit 2: a grey lump that the teacher cuts with a knife and keeps under kerosene. Exhibit 3: a very thin shiny sheet made by beating, used to decorate sweets. The organisers must put two tests on the board for deciding that a material is a metal, choosing from: hard, solid at room temperature, lustrous, malleable.
(a) Name the property shown by Exhibit 3 and the metal in Exhibit 1.
(b) Which two of the four candidate tests do Exhibits 1 and 2 break, and how?
(c) Why can the hammering test not be used on Exhibit 1?
(d) Choose the two tests for the board and justify using all three exhibits.
questions.a: (a) Malleability; mercury. (b) Exhibit 1 breaks 'solid at room temperature' (it is a liquid); Exhibit 2 breaks 'hard' (soft enough to cut with a knife). (c) A liquid cannot be beaten into a thin sheet. (d) Lustrous and malleable: exhibits 1 and 2 show that 'hard' and 'solid' fail, while the shiny appearance applies to all three exhibits and malleability to Exhibit 3. The board should say 'generally', since Exhibit 1 cannot be hammered.
s: (a) malleability and mercury
(b) liquid breaks 'solid'; soft metal breaks 'hard'
(c) a liquid cannot be hammered into a sheet
(d) lustrous and malleable chosen, with 'generally' caveat

questions.q:
Gurpreet's grandfather, a village blacksmith in Punjab, heats an iron bar in a coal furnace and beats it into a sickle blade. At school Gurpreet hammers four samples. P is shiny, hard and flattens. Q is dull, soft and breaks into pieces. R is dull and neither flattens nor breaks. S is shiny, soft enough to be cut with a knife and kept in kerosene by the teacher.
(a) Which of the samples P, Q, R and S are metals?
(b) Name the property shown by P and the property shown by Q on hammering.
(c) Gurpreet says S cannot be a metal because it is soft. Is he right? Give one reason.
(d) The blacksmith needs one material for a blade and one for its handle from P, Q and R. Choose for each and justify.
questions.a: (a) P and S are metals; Q and R are not metals (Q breaks, R neither flattens nor breaks). (b) P is malleable; Q is brittle. (c) No. Some metals such as sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife. (d) Blade: P, a hard malleable metal like iron. Handle: R, wood-like material (blacksmiths use wood for handles); Q would break.
s: (a) P and S are metals
(b) P malleable, Q brittle
(c) soft metals exist, sodium and potassium
(d) blade P, handle R, with reason

questions.q: Differentiate between a 'brittle' material and one that is 'neither malleable nor brittle', naming one material and its hammering result for each.
questions.a: A brittle material (coal or sulfur) breaks into pieces when beaten. A material that is neither (wood) neither flattens into a sheet nor breaks into pieces.
s: brittle: breaks into pieces, e.g. coal or sulfur
neither: stays whole and unflattened, e.g. wood

questions.q: A craft teacher lists three jobs: (i) making the fine mesh of a tea strainer, (ii) wrapping a sweet in thin foil, (iii) making a school bell that rings. Which option pairs every job with the property it needs?
questions.a: Strainer mesh needs wires, so ductility; foil needs sheets, so malleability; the ringing bell needs sonority.
o: Ductility, malleability, sonority
Malleability, ductility, sonority
Ductility, sonority, malleability
Sonority, malleability, ductility

questions.q: Ravi taps four equal discs in a bag. Discs E and G ring and discs F and H give a dull thud. He announces, 'E and G have been drawn into wires, so they are ductile.' What is wrong with his reasoning?
questions.a: A ringing sound shows sonority, which is a property of metals; it says nothing about whether the metal can be drawn into wires.
o: Ringing shows sonority, not ductility
Ringing shows that E and G are brittle
A dull thud shows F and H are ductile
A thud shows F and H are malleable

questions.q: Sneha, who cannot see, walks down a lane tapping a stick. Near a steel pole she hears a ringing sound; near a wooden pole she hears a dull sound. Which pair of objects could she NOT tell apart by tapping?
questions.a: A lump of coal and a block of wood both give dull sounds, so the sound cannot separate them. Each of the other pairs has one ringing and one dull object.
o: Coal lump and wooden block
Steel pole and wooden pole
Metal coin and wooden block
Steel plate and coal lump

questions.q: Which statement about wires and ropes is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Steel is a mixture of iron and carbon, and ropes of steel wires are used on cranes and bridges, so containing a non-metal does not stop steel being drawn into wire.
o: Steel cannot be drawn into wires as it holds a non-metal
Ropes made of steel wires can support heavy loads on cranes
Copper and aluminium wires are used in electrical fittings
Some bangles and necklaces are made from metal wires

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Steel ropes are used in cranes to lift heavy objects.
Reason (R): Steel is a pure metal, which is why it can be drawn into strong wires.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, since ropes of steel wires support heavy loads. R is false: steel is a mixture of a metal (iron) and a non-metal (carbon), not a pure metal.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about wires and sound.
Statement 1: Copper and aluminium wires are used in electrical fittings because metals are sonorous.
Statement 2: Steel is a mixture of iron, a metal, and carbon, a non-metal.
Statement 3: The ringing of a school bell is due to the sonority of metals.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are true. 1 is false: metal wires exist because metals are ductile; sonority is the ringing property.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A jeweller needs a gold wire 500 m long. Using the fact that 1 g of gold can be drawn into a 2 km wire (same thickness), the gold needed is ___ g.
True or False: A sheet of aluminium foil shows that aluminium is ductile. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. A foil is a thin sheet made by beating, which shows malleability. Ductility would be shown by drawing the metal into a wire.
s: verdict: false
foil shows malleability, ductility needs a wire

questions.q:
A visually impaired student finds her way by tapping a stick on what is around her.
(a) Why does a steel railing sound different from a wooden door?
(b) Would tapping help her tell a lump of coal from a block of wood? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Metals are sonorous and give a ringing sound; wood gives a dull sound. (b) No: coal and wood both give dull sounds, so the sound cannot separate them.
s: (a) metal rings (sonority), wood dull
(b) coal and wood both dull, so no

questions.q:
A goldsmith makes a thin leaf to decorate an idol and a fine wire for an earring from the same gold.
(a) Name the property used for the leaf and the property used for the wire.
(b) Which of these two properties does the figure '1 g of gold gives a 2 km line' illustrate?
questions.a: (a) Leaf: malleability. Wire: ductility. (b) Ductility, because a long line of gold is a drawn wire.
s: (a) malleability for leaf, ductility for wire
(b) the 2 km figure illustrates ductility

questions.q:
A sitar string has to be a wire that also rings when plucked or struck.
(a) Name the two properties of metals a sitar string uses.
(b) Which of the two would a thin strip of dry wood lack, even if it were cut as thin as a string?
questions.a: (a) Ductility (it is a wire) and sonority (it rings). (b) Sonority: wood gives a dull sound; wood is also not ductile, so it cannot be drawn into a wire.
s: (a) ductility and sonority
(b) wood gives a dull sound instead of ringing

questions.q: A student says, 'Ductility and sonority are the same because a metal wire rings when it is pulled tight.' (a) State what each word means. (b) Give a metal object that uses only one of them.
questions.a: (a) Ductility: being drawn into wires; sonority: giving a ringing sound when struck. (b) Examples: a school bell (sonority only) or a tea-strainer mesh or electrical wire (ductility).
s: (a) ductility is drawing into wires, sonority is ringing
(b) an object using only one property

questions.q: Imran says, 'Ductility is mainly possessed by metals, and steel contains carbon, a non-metal. So steel cannot be drawn into wires.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. The chapter says ropes are made of steel wires, so steel is drawn into wires. It also says ductility is 'mainly' a property of metals, and steel is a mixture of a metal (iron) with carbon, so containing a non-metal does not rule it out.
s: verdict: no
ropes of steel wires exist, so steel is ductile
steel is mostly iron with carbon; 'mainly' is not 'only'

questions.q: A seller offers 'sulfur strings' for a violin. Show, using two properties from the chapter, why such strings cannot work.
questions.a: Sulfur is not ductile, so it cannot be drawn into a wire (we never see wires of coal or sulfur). It is also not sonorous, so it would not give a ringing sound; the chapter notes sulfur and coal break into pieces.
s: not ductile, so no wire can be drawn
not sonorous, so no ringing sound
brittle: breaks into pieces instead

questions.q: Write a short word problem about gold wire that uses the figure '1 g of gold gives a 2 km wire', needs a change of units, and solve it.
questions.a: Example: How much gold is needed for a 750 m thread? 750 m = 0.75 km; 0.75 / 2 = 0.375 g. (Any correct problem and correct working: setting up the ratio, converting metres to km, and the answer.)
s: problem uses 2 km per gram
converts metres to kilometres correctly
correct final answer in grams

questions.q: A craft stall displays: (1) a copper wire in a plug, (2) a coin, (3) silver foil on a sweet, (4) a sitar string, (5) a tea strainer of wire mesh, (6) a lump of coal. Sort the items by whether they rely on ductility, malleability or sonority. Say which item relies on two properties, and why the lump of coal fails all three.
questions.a: Ductility: copper wire, sitar string, tea strainer. Malleability: silver foil. Sonority: coin (rings when dropped) and the sitar string. The sitar string relies on two (wire and ringing). Coal cannot be drawn into wire (not ductile), breaks into pieces instead of flattening (brittle) and gives a dull sound (not sonorous).
s: ductility: copper wire, sitar string and strainer mesh
malleability: silver foil
sonority: coin, and also the sitar string
sitar string relies on two properties
coal is not ductile, not malleable (brittle) and not sonorous

questions.q: A goldsmith in Jaipur is asked for a 3.6 km gold thread for a temple decoration. He has 1.5 g of gold. Using 1 g of gold gives a 2 km wire of the same thickness, find the gold needed, the shortfall, and the longest thread he can make from 1.5 g. Name the property involved, state the assumption you are making, and advise whether he should shorten the thread or buy more gold, giving a reason.
questions.a: Gold needed: 3.6 / 2 = 1.8 g. Shortfall: 1.8 - 1.5 = 0.3 g. Longest thread: 1.5 x 2 = 3 km. The property is ductility. Assumption: the same thickness of wire. Advice: either choice is valid if justified; for example, buy 0.3 g more if a 3.6 km thread is needed, or shorten to 3 km if cost matters.
s: gold needed 1.8 g
shortfall 0.3 g
longest thread 3 km
property ductility, assumption same thickness
advice with a reason

questions.q: A tapping test shows plate X rings and plate Y gives a dull thud. Explain what each result suggests, and why a second property should still be checked before declaring X a metal.
questions.a: Ringing suggests X is sonorous like metals; a dull sound suggests Y is like coal or wood. One property alone is not enough, so a second one (such as conduction in a tester circuit or flattening on beating) should be checked.
s: X rings: sonorous, like metals
Y dull: like coal or wood
a second property should be checked

questions.q:
A goldsmith in Thrissur has 3 g of gold. One customer wants a fine wire 450 m long for a chain and thin leaf for a small idol from the rest. A second customer brings only 0.5 g and wants a 1.2 km wire. Use the chapter's figure that 1 g of gold can be drawn into a 2 km wire.
(a) Name the property used for the wire and the property used for the leaf.
(b) How many grams does the 450 m wire need, and how much gold is left for the leaf?
(c) How many grams does the second customer's 1.2 km wire need, and by how much is she short?
(d) Advise the second customer: shorten the wire or add gold? Justify using your numbers.
questions.a: (a) Ductility for the wire; malleability for the leaf. (b) 0.45 km / 2 = 0.225 g; 3 - 0.225 = 2.775 g left. (c) 1.2 / 2 = 0.6 g; short by 0.1 g. (d) Either is acceptable with a reason: shortening to 1 km (0.5 g) keeps her cost the same; adding 0.1 g gives the full 1.2 km. The decision depends on whether length or cost matters more.
s: (a) ductility and malleability
(c) 0.6 g and short by 0.1 g
(d) justified choice using the numbers

questions.q:
The music club of a school in Chennai needs a bell plate. All four plates on the shop counter look silver. When tapped, plate P rings, Q gives a dull thud, R rings and S gives a dull thud. The shopkeeper says plates with a ringing sound are the metal ones. The club has a tester circuit (a cell, a bulb and wires) that costs nothing to use.
(a) Which plates are likely metal, and which property did the tapping show?
(b) Why can looking at the plates not settle the matter here?
(c) The club decides to add a tester test on P and R. What result would support that they are metals?
(d) The club chairman says tapping alone is enough and the tester is a waste of time. Decide whether you agree and justify.
questions.a: (a) P and R are likely metals; the property is sonority. (b) All four look alike, so appearance gives no difference, whereas sound does. (c) The bulb glows: the chapter found that all the materials that made the bulb glow were metals. (d) Disagree: tapping tests only one property; adding a second, free test makes the conclusion safer. (A reasoned agreement that notes the cost and time of the tester should be credited only if it admits that one property is a pattern, not proof.)
s: (a) P and R, sonority
(b) all look alike; the sound separates them
(c) bulb glows for a metal
(d) decision with reason about one property versus two

questions.q: A music teacher replaces a broken violin string with a thin metal wire. A student says the same metal beaten into a narrow strip would do as well. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: The wire is possible because metals are ductile; a strip comes from beating, which uses malleability, so it is a different shape made by a different property.
o: A string needs ductility; a beaten strip shows malleability, not a wire
A string needs sonority; a strip cannot ring at all
A string needs brittleness, so a strip is the better choice
A string needs malleability, so the strip is the same thing

questions.q: In a tester circuit, an unknown dull grey rod makes the bulb glow. Using only the pattern found in the chapter's electricity activity, which conclusion is best?
questions.a: It is a good conductor of electricity, and since every material that made the bulb glow was a metal, it is probably a metal, though other properties should be checked.
o: Probably a metal, to be confirmed by other tests
Certainly a metal, so no other test is needed
A poor conductor, because it is not shiny at all
A conductor of heat alone, not of electricity

questions.q: Kabir dips a thick metal spoon into cold water and a thin wooden spoon into hot water. After five minutes the wooden spoon's top end feels warmer. He concludes that wood conducts heat better than metal. What is wrong with his test?
questions.a: The spoons were in water of different temperatures and had different thickness, so the difference may not be due to the material; Activity 4.3 uses spoons of almost the same size in the same hot water for the same time.
o: The water temperatures and spoon sizes differed
Metal spoons cannot be put into any water
He should have used a tester circuit for this
The wooden spoon was left in for too long

questions.q: A student reads the tester results (the bulb glowed for aluminium foil, iron nail and copper wire, and stayed off for sulfur, coal, dry wood, stone, rubber eraser and nylon rope). Which of her conclusions is NOT supported by those results?
questions.a: The tester shows electrical conduction only; it gives no information about conduction of heat, so a conclusion about heat is unsupported.
o: Sulfur and coal are poor conductors of heat
Dry wood is a poor conductor of electricity
Aluminium foil is a good conductor of electricity
Every item that made the bulb glow was a metal

questions.q: Aditi sees that the top end of a wooden stick dipped in hot water stays cool, and says, 'So the tester bulb will also stay off if I connect this stick.' Which statement about her reasoning is correct?
questions.a: Her prediction happens to match the tester result for dry wood, but the water test shows only conduction of heat; the tester has to be used to show conduction of electricity.
o: The water test shows heat only; the tester is needed for electricity
The water test already proves wood is a poor conductor of electricity
The tester cannot be used for a stick, only for metal objects
Heat and electricity always behave the same way in every material

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The plastic covering on a screwdriver handle protects an electrician from a burn.
Reason (R): Plastic is a poor conductor of electricity.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter says the plastic covering protects from electric shock, not from burns. R is true.
o: A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q:
Read the statements about conduction.
Statement 1: In Activity 4.3 the two spoons are kept in water at the same temperature for the same time, so any difference comes from the material.
Statement 2: Materials that allow electricity to flow through them easily are called good conductors of electricity.
Statement 3: Wooden handles are fixed on metal vessels because wood is also a good conductor of heat.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are true. 3 is false: wooden handles are used because wood is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle does not get hot.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. The top end of a metal spoon in hot water is hotter than that of a wooden spoon. 2. The tester bulb stays off when a rubber eraser is in the gap. 3. The tester bulb glows when an iron nail is in the gap. 4. A cook holds a pan by a wooden handle without being burnt.
Column II: a. Rubber is a poor conductor of electricity. b. Iron is a good conductor of electricity. c. Wood is a poor conductor of heat. d. Metal is a good conductor of heat.
Choose the correct pairing.

In the same hot water, the top end of a metal spoon rises from 30 degrees C to 60 degrees C, while that of a wooden spoon rises from 30 degrees C to 36 degrees C. The metal spoon's rise is ___ times that of the wooden spoon.
True or False: When a rubber eraser is placed in the gap of a tester circuit and the bulb stays off, this supports the use of rubber gloves by an electrician. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The bulb staying off shows that rubber is a poor conductor of electricity, and the chapter says rubber gloves protect the electrician from electric shock for this reason.
s: verdict: true
rubber is a poor conductor of electricity, so it blocks shock

questions.q:
In Activity 4.3 the spoons are of 'almost the same size and thickness' and are put in the same hot water for the same time.
(a) Name two things kept the same.
(b) Why must they be kept the same before saying that metal conducts heat better than wood?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: size/thickness of the spoons, temperature of the water, time in the water. (b) Then the only difference is the material, so the hotter metal spoon shows that metal conducts heat better.
s: (a) two conditions kept same
(b) only the material differs, so the difference is due to it

questions.q:
An electrician's screwdriver has a metal tip and a plastic handle.
(a) Name the part that protects the electrician and the property that lets it do so.
(b) What would be the danger if the handle were also made of iron?
questions.a: (a) The plastic handle (covering): plastic is a poor conductor of electricity. (b) Iron is a good conductor of electricity, so current could pass through the handle to the electrician's hand and give an electric shock.
s: (a) plastic covering, poor conductor of electricity
(b) iron conducts electricity, so shock

questions.q: Two classmates use the words 'conduction' and 'conductor' loosely. Using the spoon activity, say which word names the process, which names the material, and what the metal spoon showed.
questions.a: Conduction is the transfer of heat from one point to another in a material; a conductor is the material that transfers heat. The metal spoon is a good conductor, so conduction took heat from the water to its upper end.
s: conduction is the process of heat transfer
conductor is the material; metal spoon is a good conductor

questions.q:
A cook leaves a metal ladle standing in a pot of boiling dal while she chops onions.
(a) What will she feel when she picks it up by the upper end?
(b) Name the process by which the upper end became so, and say what would differ if the ladle were wooden.
questions.a: (a) The upper end will be hot. (b) Conduction: heat transferred through the metal from the hot dal. A wooden ladle, a poor conductor of heat, would transfer heat poorly and its upper end would stay much cooler.
s: (a) the upper end is hot
(b) conduction through metal; wood would stay cooler as a poor conductor

questions.q: Meena tests an iron nail in a tester circuit and the bulb glows. She says, 'So every metal is a good conductor of electricity.' Is she right, and is her evidence enough?
questions.a: Partly. The chapter's pattern (aluminium, iron and copper all made the bulb glow) supports that metals are generally good conductors, but one nail alone is not enough to say every metal. Several materials must be tested to see a pattern.
s: verdict: partly right
the pattern across aluminium, iron and copper supports 'generally'
one nail is not enough for 'every'

questions.q: Sunil says, 'A wooden handle stays cool on a hot pan because wood is a poor conductor of electricity; the tester bulb stays off with dry wood.' Do you agree?
questions.a: No. The tester bulb stays off for dry wood, which shows poor conduction of electricity. A cool handle depends on conduction of heat, which the spoon activity shows: wood transfers heat poorly. The two properties are tested separately.
s: verdict: no
the tester shows electrical conduction only
the cool handle is explained by wood being a poor conductor of heat (spoon activity)

questions.q: Describe one everyday situation not given in the chapter in which a poor conductor of heat is needed, and one in which a poor conductor of electricity is needed. Give the reason in each.
questions.a: Examples: oven gloves (cloth) so that hot trays do not burn the hands, because cloth conducts heat poorly; a rubber cover on a power-cable wire so that touching it does not give a shock, because rubber is a poor conductor of electricity.
s: a valid situation for a poor conductor of heat
a valid situation for a poor conductor of electricity
a reason in terms of conduction for each

questions.q: Rukmini tests two unlabelled objects in a tester. The bulb glows for X, a dull black rod, and stays off for W, a shiny plate. Using the chapter's pattern, what does she conclude about X? What does she make of W, and what should she do next?
questions.a: All materials that made the bulb glow in the chapter were metals, so X is probably a metal, to be checked by other properties. W is shiny but did not let the bulb glow, which does not fit the usual pattern, so she should re-check the circuit and test W's other properties before classifying it.
s: X: probably a metal, since glowing materials were metals
W: does not fit the pattern
next step: re-check the circuit and other properties

questions.q: Zoya tests an iron key, an aluminium spoon, a plastic scale, a wooden pencil and a stone in a tester circuit. Predict which will make the bulb glow. Then a rod she cannot name also makes the bulb glow. Say what you can and cannot conclude about it from the chapter, and why one result is not enough to decide.
questions.a: Glow: iron key and aluminium spoon. No glow: plastic scale, wooden pencil, stone. The rod that glows is a good conductor of electricity and, since all the materials that glowed were metals, it is likely a metal. The pattern is only a pattern, so more properties (lustre, malleability) should be checked before deciding.
s: iron key and aluminium spoon glow
plastic scale, pencil and stone do not glow
the rod is a good conductor of electricity
likely a metal since the glowing materials were metals
one result is not enough; check more properties

questions.q: A hostel is buying an electric kettle. For each part, say whether it should be a good or a poor conductor, of heat or of electricity, name a suitable kind of material from the chapter, and give the reason: (i) the body where water is heated, (ii) the handle held by the cook, (iii) the plug pin, (iv) the outer covering of the cable. Then state which of the four parts has to be good at one kind of conduction while a neighbouring part has to be poor at the same kind.
questions.a: (i) Body: good conductor of heat, a metal, so heat reaches the water. (ii) Handle: poor conductor of heat, wood or a similar material, so the hand is not burnt. (iii) Pin: good conductor of electricity, a metal, so current reaches the kettle. (iv) Cable covering: poor conductor of electricity, plastic or rubber, so the user is protected from shock. The pin (good) and the cable covering (poor) both concern conduction of electricity side by side.
s: (i) metal body, good heat conductor
(ii) wood-like handle, poor heat conductor
(iii) metal pin, good electrical conductor
(iv) plastic or rubber covering, poor electrical conductor
pin versus covering: opposite needs for electrical conduction

questions.q:
The kitchen of a hostel in Nagpur must buy 18 cooking pots. Pot M has a metal handle and costs ₹250. Pot W has a wooden handle and costs ₹320. To compare handles, a student puts a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in the same hot water. After 5 minutes the top end of the metal spoon has risen from 30 to 58 degrees C and the wooden spoon from 30 to 33 degrees C. The cook says she can hold a metal handle with a cloth.
(a) By how many degrees did each spoon's top end rise, and what does the result show?
(b) How much more would the hostel pay for 18 pots with wooden handles?
(c) The maker of Pot W advertises, 'Cool handle, because wood does not conduct electricity.' Is the reason correct?
(d) Decide between Pot M and Pot W and justify, using your numbers.
questions.a: (a) Metal 28 degrees, wooden 3 degrees: metal conducts heat well, wood poorly. (b) 18 x (320 - 250) = 18 x 70 = ₹1,260. (c) No. The handle stays cool because wood is a poor conductor of heat, as the spoon result shows; conduction of electricity is a different property, tested with the tester. (d) Either choice can be justified: Pot W costs ₹1,260 more but needs no cloth, a safer handle; Pot M saves ₹1,260 but its handle heats up as the metal spoon did, so cloths must always be used. A safety-first answer chooses Pot W.
s: (a) rises 28 and 3 degrees; metal conducts heat, wood poorly
(c) reason wrong: heat conduction, not electricity
(d) reasoned decision using cost and safety

questions.q:
Rukmini builds a small model with a cell, a bulb and wires. She tests five objects in the gap of her tester. A copper wire and an iron nail make the bulb glow; a nylon rope, a rubber eraser and a piece of dry wood do not. She needs (i) leads to carry current, (ii) a covering for the leads and (iii) a knob for a switch that sits near a warm bulb. The nylon rope costs ₹5, the eraser ₹3 and the wood ₹8. She also puts a wooden spoon in hot water and finds its top end stays cool; she has no heat results for the nylon rope or the eraser.
(a) Which objects suit the leads, and which the covering?
(b) Which property does the knob need if it is to be safe for her hand, and from which tests is that known?
(c) Which of the three objects can the knob be made from using only the evidence she has?
(d) The cheapest is the eraser at ₹3. Should she choose it? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Leads: copper wire and iron nail (good conductors); covering: nylon rope, eraser or dry wood (poor conductors of electricity). (b) Poor conductor of electricity (tester) and of heat (spoon test). (c) Dry wood, the only one shown poor for both. (d) Choose wood even though it costs ₹5 more than the eraser: the eraser and nylon were only shown to be poor conductors of electricity, and nothing in the evidence shows they are poor conductors of heat near a warm bulb. (A reasoned choice of the cheaper eraser should mention that its heat behaviour is untested.)
s: (a) metals for leads; nylon, eraser or wood for covering
(b) poor conductor of electricity and of heat, from the tester and spoon tests
(c) dry wood
(d) decision weighs cost against missing heat evidence

questions.q: Neha sets up three bottles. X: a nail with silica gel, tightly capped. Y: a nail in freshly boiled and cooled water with a layer of oil, tightly capped. Z: a nail partly in water in an open bottle. After 10 days which nails show brown deposits?
questions.a: Rust needs air and water together. X has no moisture, Y has no air; only Z has both.
o: Only the nail in Z
The nails in X and Z
Only the nail in X
The nails in X, Y and Z

questions.q: A store keeper keeps iron nails in two ways. Box 1 is sealed and holds silica gel packets. Box 2 is open and sits near a leaking tap. After some weeks which result is expected, and why?
questions.a: Box 2 nails get brown rust because moist air (water and air together) is present; in Box 1 the air is dry, so brown deposits do not develop.
o: Only Box 2 nails rust: air and water both reach them
Only Box 1 nails rust, because they are shut in with air
Both boxes rust equally, because iron always rusts in time
Neither box rusts, because a leaking tap gives water only

questions.q: Two iron buckets stand in a school garden through the monsoon. One is plain; the other has a thin coating of zinc. Only the plain bucket develops brown patches. Which explanation uses the chapter correctly?
questions.a: The zinc coating (galvanisation) is a protective layer on the iron; it is not an oil layer, not silica gel and not a way of boiling the rain water.
o: Zinc is a protective layer put on the iron by galvanisation
A layer of oil was floating on the coated bucket's rain water
Zinc kept the rain water boiled and free of dissolved gases
Zinc acted like silica gel and dried the air around the bucket

questions.q: A student predicts the result of four set-ups with iron nails. Which prediction is WRONG?
questions.a: Without the oil layer, air can dissolve again into the boiled water, and the bottle is open, so the nail meets air and water and may rust. The other three predictions follow the experiment.
o: A nail in boiled water with no oil, open bottle, stays rust-free
A nail in a capped bottle with silica gel stays free of rust
A nail in boiled water under a layer of oil stays free of rust
A nail partly dipped in water in an open bottle will rust

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Iron Pillar of Delhi has barely any rust after more than 1600 years.
Reason (R): The Iron Pillar of Delhi is about 8 metres high and weighs more than 6000 kilograms.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but its height and weight do not explain the lack of rust; the chapter says the pillar was made in a way that resists rusting.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about rusting.
Statement 1: A nail in boiled and cooled water under a layer of oil shows a brown deposit because water is present.
Statement 2: The black coating that forms on silver objects is called rust.
Statement 3: Applying a protective layer of zinc on iron is called galvanisation.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only 3 is correct. In 1 the nail has no air, so no brown deposit forms; in 2 rust is the brown deposit on iron, and the black coating on silver is a case of corrosion.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Match each set-up in Column I with its expected result in Column II.
Column I: 1. A nail sealed in a bottle with silica gel. 2. A nail under oil in boiled, cooled water in a capped bottle. 3. A nail partly in water in an open bottle. 4. A greased nail standing in damp air.
Column II: a. No rust: water is missing. b. No rust: air is missing. c. Rusts: air and water both reach the nail. d. No rust: a protective layer keeps both away.
Choose the correct pairing.

Five nails are left for ten days. N1: sealed with silica gel. N2: boiled, cooled water under oil, capped. N3: open bottle, partly dipped in water. N4: outside on a balcony in damp monsoon air. N5: sealed with silica gel in a dry box. The number that rust is ___.
True or False: An iron nail dipped fully in water, with no air at all, would still develop a brown deposit at the same rate as a nail in moist air. Justify your verdict with the chapter's experiment.
questions.a: False. In bottle B (boiled and cooled water with a layer of oil, tightly capped) the nail shows no brown deposit; both air and water must be present.
s: verdict: false
bottle B had water but no air and did not rust, so both are needed

questions.q:
A tourist says the Iron Pillar of Delhi has little rust because Delhi has no rain or wind.
(a) What does the chapter say the pillar has faced for more than 1600 years?
(b) What does the chapter say its lack of rust shows?
questions.a: (a) Winds, rainfall and intense weather. (b) That it was made in a way that resists rusting, which tells us about the skill developed in metal technology in India.
s: (a) winds, rainfall and intense weather
(b) made to resist rusting, showing skill in metal technology

questions.q:
A cycle chain is wiped with oil every month.
(a) Which method of preventing rust is this?
(b) Using the two conditions for rusting, explain how it helps.
questions.a: (a) Oiling. (b) Rust needs air and water together; the oil forms a layer on the iron that keeps moist air off the metal, so the two conditions do not act on the chain together.
s: (a) oiling
(b) layer keeps air and water from reaching the iron

questions.q:
A student puts an iron nail partly in water in a bottle and screws the cap on tightly. She says, 'The cap keeps air out, so the nail will not rust.'
(a) Predict what will happen and give the reason.
(b) State how bottle B of the chapter's experiment avoided the same mistake.
questions.a: (a) The nail will rust: the closed bottle still contains air, and the nail is in contact with both air and water. (b) In bottle B the water was boiled and cooled to remove dissolved gases, and a layer of oil stopped air dissolving into the water.
s: (a) rusts, because sealed-in air and water are both present
(b) boiling removed dissolved gases and oil blocked air

questions.q:
A copper tap develops a green coating and an iron tap a brown one.
(a) Which coating is called rust?
(b) What general word covers both, and what does it mean?
questions.a: (a) The brown deposit on the iron tap. (b) Corrosion: gradual deterioration of metal surfaces caused by air, water or other substances.
s: (a) brown deposit on iron
(b) corrosion and its meaning

questions.q: Asha says, 'If I pour away the oil from bottle B and leave the bottle open, with the nail still partly dipped, the nail will rust after some days.' Do you agree? Explain with the activity.
questions.a: Yes. The oil layer had stopped air dissolving into the boiled water. Without it, and with the bottle open, air reaches the nail and the water, so both conditions are present and the nail rusts, as in bottle C.
s: verdict: yes
the oil layer was blocking air
with oil gone and the bottle open, air and water are both present, as in bottle C

questions.q: Ajay says the black coating on his silver ring is rust. Is he right?
questions.a: No. Rust is the brown deposit on objects made of iron, and silver is not iron. The black coating on silver is corrosion, the gradual damage of a metal surface by air, water or other substances.
s: verdict: no
rust is the brown deposit on iron
the black coating is corrosion

questions.q: Mrinal argues, 'The Iron Pillar of Delhi has stood in the open for more than 1600 years, so iron simply does not rust in the open.' Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: In Activity 4.5 an iron nail rusts when it meets both air and water, and iron objects left in the open develop brown deposits within a few days. The pillar is an exception that the chapter explains by saying it was made in a way that resists rusting, so one lasting object cannot show that iron never rusts.
s: iron objects in the open rust (nail in bottle C)
the pillar has barely any rust, not none
it was made to resist rusting; one object does not prove a rule

questions.q: Describe an experiment of your own, different from the chapter's three bottles, in which an iron nail stays in contact with both air and water and still does not rust. Name the method you use.
questions.a: Example: coat the nail thickly with grease (or oil it, or paint it, or zinc-coat it) and leave it partly dipped in water in an open bottle. The protective layer keeps the iron from direct contact with air and water, so it does not rust. Method: greasing (or oiling, painting, galvanisation).
s: a set-up with air and water both present
a protective layer on the nail
the method is named

questions.q: Two new bottles are set up with iron nails. Bottle D has a nail partly dipped in freshly boiled and cooled water with no oil on top, left open. Bottle E has a nail coated thickly with grease, left open in a dish of water. Predict what you expect for D and for E after 10 days, with reasons. Then say what the pair tells you about conditions for rusting.
questions.a: D: the nail will rust, since without the oil layer air can dissolve in the water and the part of the nail above water meets air directly, so both air and water are present. E: the nail will not rust, since grease is a protective layer that prevents contact with air and water. The pair shows rust needs both air and water together and a protective layer prevents it.
s: D rusts
reason for D: air and water both present
E does not rust
reason for E: grease layer
conclusion from the pair

questions.q: A school stands in a hill town. Its iron gate is in the open and gets rain for five months. Its stationery racks (iron) are inside a sealed, dry cupboard with silica gel packets. Its iron swings stand in the playground. For each, say whether rusting is likely and which of the two conditions are present or absent. For the gate, then choose between painting and galvanisation and give a reason based on what the chapter says rusting costs the country.
questions.a: Gate: likely to rust; rain gives water and the open air gives air. Racks: unlikely; silica gel keeps the air dry, so water is missing. Swings: likely to rust in the open, like the gate. For the gate a protective layer is needed; galvanisation (zinc) or painting both qualify. An enormous amount of money is spent every year on replacing or repairing rusted iron, so a durable protection is worth its cost.
s: gate likely to rust, air and water present
racks unlikely: dry air, water missing
swings likely to rust in the open
a protective method chosen for the gate
reason links to the money lost to rusting

questions.q:
A school keeps 30 iron hurdles. During the monsoon they get wet. Plan 1: put them in a tightly shut store with silica gel packets at ₹150 per month. Plan 2: paint them twice a year at ₹1,100 each time and leave them in the open verandah. The sports teacher says the store door must be opened every day because students take hurdles out for practice, and the monsoon air outside is very damp.
(a) Which condition for rusting does silica gel remove?
(b) Why may Plan 1 work less well than its cost suggests?
(c) Work out the cost of each plan for one year.
(d) Decide between the two plans and justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Water (moisture): silica gel keeps the air dry. (b) Opening the door every day lets damp air in, so the air in the store will not stay dry. (c) Plan 1: 150 x 12 = ₹1,800. Plan 2: 1,100 x 2 = ₹2,200. (d) Plan 1 is ₹400 cheaper but only protects if the store stays closed; Plan 2 costs more yet does not depend on the door. A reasoned choice either way is accepted: Plan 2 if the door must keep opening, Plan 1 if practice can be organised so that the door opens rarely.
s: (a) water or moisture removed
(b) opening the door lets damp air in
(d) decision weighing the ₹400 saving against reliability

questions.q:
Mansi visits the Iron Pillar of Delhi and notes that it has barely any rust. Her grandfather's iron gate has brown patches after a few monsoons, worst where rain collects. A dealer offers painting at ₹2,500 every year, or galvanisation at ₹12,000 once, which he says will last at least 5 years. The family has little spare money each year but has some savings.
(a) Which two conditions has the pillar faced outdoors that make iron rust?
(b) Which of the two conditions does the rain supply to the gate?
(c) Name the zinc-coating process and work out which option costs less over 5 years.
(d) Which option would you advise? Give your decision and reasons.
questions.a: (a) Air and water (from rain). (b) Water. (c) Galvanisation. Painting: 5 x 2,500 = ₹12,500 against ₹12,000 once, so galvanisation costs ₹500 less if the dealer is right. (d) Either is acceptable with a reason: galvanisation is cheaper over 5 years if the family can pay ₹12,000 now; painting spreads the cost if savings are needed, but costs ₹500 more and must be repeated yearly.
s: (a) air and water
(b) rain supplies water
(c) galvanisation; ₹12,500 against ₹12,000
(d) reasoned decision on lump sum against yearly cost

questions.q: Kavita finds a soft, dull grey solid. A small piece placed in water shows no reaction at all, and the same solid does not light a tester bulb. How should she classify it?
questions.a: As a non-metal, like sulfur: soft and dull, it does not react with water and is a poor conductor. Sodium would react vigorously with water.
o: A non-metal: no reaction with water and a poor conductor
A metal like sodium: it is soft, so it must be metal
A metal like mercury: being dull, it must be a stable metal
Neither: any soft dull solid is not an element at all

questions.q: By mistake a lab assistant drops a piece of sodium into the trough of water in which phosphorus is kept. What does the chapter lead you to expect?
questions.a: Sodium reacts vigorously with water, and a lot of heat is generated. This is why sodium is stored in kerosene and not in water.
o: A vigorous reaction that gives out a lot of heat
Nothing happens, as for phosphorus in water
The sodium catches fire only after it leaves the water
A slow change that makes the water acidic

questions.q: A teacher drops a pinch of sulfur into water: nothing happens. She then burns another pinch in a gas jar, covers it, shakes the gas with water and dips blue and red litmus papers. Which description of what the class sees is correct?
questions.a: Sulfur itself does not react with water, but its oxide (sulfur dioxide) dissolved in water gives an acid, so blue litmus turns red and red litmus stays red.
o: The pinch in water shows no reaction; the jar solution turns blue litmus red
The pinch in water turns blue litmus red; the jar solution shows no change at all
Both the pinch in water and the jar solution turn red litmus paper blue
Neither the pinch in water nor the jar solution changes either litmus paper

questions.q: Anil burns magnesium ribbon and collects the white powder; Pooja burns sulfur in a closed jar. Each dissolves her product in water and dips both blue and red litmus. Which table of results is correct?
questions.a: Magnesium oxide is basic: red litmus turns blue and blue stays blue. The sulfur solution is acidic: blue litmus turns red and red stays red.
o: Anil: red turns blue. Pooja: blue turns red
Anil: blue turns red. Pooja: red turns blue
Anil: red turns blue. Pooja: red turns blue
Anil: blue turns red. Pooja: blue turns red

questions.q: A student writes four lines in her record of the burning-sulfur demonstration. Which line is INCORRECT?
questions.a: Sulfur powder placed directly in water shows no reaction, so no acidic solution forms; the acid forms only from the gas made by burning sulfur.
o: Sulfur placed directly in water turns blue litmus red
The gas formed on burning sulfur dissolves in water on shaking
The demonstration is done in a fume hood or ventilated room
The solution of the gas turns blue litmus paper red

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The oxide of sodium is expected to turn red litmus blue.
Reason (R): Sodium is a metal, and oxides of metals are generally basic in nature.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: a metal's oxide is generally basic, and a basic solution turns red litmus blue.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about storage and classification.
Statement 1: Sodium is stored in kerosene to keep it away from air and moisture.
Statement 2: Phosphorus is stored in water because it reacts vigorously with water.
Statement 3: Plastic and glass are non-metals because they are not metals.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. Phosphorus is kept in water because it catches fire in air, not because it reacts with water; plastic and glass are not classified as non-metals because they are not elements.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: Among sodium, sulfur, magnesium and phosphorus burnt in air, the number of elements whose oxides are expected to be basic in nature is ___.
True or False: Sulfur does not react with water, yet the solution obtained by burning sulfur and shaking the gas with water can turn blue litmus red. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Sulfur by itself does not react with water, but burning it gives sulfur dioxide, whose solution in water is sulfurous acid; an acid turns blue litmus red.
s: verdict: true
the oxide formed on burning, not sulfur itself, gives the acid

questions.q:
(a) Why is sodium stored in kerosene?
(b) Using your answer, explain why sodium cannot be kept in water the way phosphorus is.
questions.a: (a) It reacts vigorously with oxygen and water, releasing a lot of heat; kerosene keeps out air and moisture. (b) Sodium reacts vigorously with water, whereas phosphorus does not react with water and only needs to be kept away from air.
s: (a) reacts vigorously with oxygen and water; kerosene keeps them out
(b) water would react with sodium, but not with phosphorus

questions.q:
The oxide of element G turns red litmus blue when dissolved in water; the oxide of element H turns blue litmus red.
(a) Which of G and H is more likely to be a metal, and by what rule?
(b) Name one property you would check next to be sure about H.
questions.a: (a) G: oxides of metals are generally basic, and a basic solution turns red litmus blue. (b) For H, check that it is dull, not malleable, not ductile, not sonorous, or a poor conductor of heat or electricity, as non-metals are.
s: (a) G, by the rule that metal oxides are generally basic
(b) a property of non-metals such as poor conduction or not malleable

questions.q:
A list reads: oxygen, wood, carbon, glass, paper, nitrogen.
(a) Which of these are elements?
(b) How many of the elements are metals, and why can the others not be called non-metals?
questions.a: (a) Oxygen, carbon and nitrogen. (b) None is a metal. Wood, glass and paper are not elements, so they are classified neither as metals nor as non-metals.
s: (a) oxygen, carbon and nitrogen
(b) no metals; wood, glass and paper are not elements

questions.q:
(a) Name the gas formed when sulfur burns in air and say what it forms with water.
(b) Why is this not a contradiction of the finding that sulfur does not react with water?
questions.a: (a) Sulfur dioxide, which forms sulfurous acid with water. (b) Sulfur and sulfur dioxide are different substances: sulfur powder placed in water does not react, but its oxide, made by burning, does dissolve in water.
s: (a) sulfur dioxide gives sulfurous acid
(b) the element does not react with water; its oxide does

questions.q: Rohit says, 'Phosphorus is a non-metal, so without any test I can predict that its oxide, dissolved in water, will turn blue litmus red.' Is his reasoning sound?
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says phosphorus behaves like sulfur and is a non-metal, and oxides of non-metals are acidic, so its oxide solution is expected to turn blue litmus red. The prediction is based on the rule, which is stated for metals and non-metals in general.
s: verdict: yes
phosphorus is a non-metal
oxides of non-metals are acidic, so blue litmus turns red

questions.q: Pooja says, 'Magnesium burns in air, so it must be a non-metal; metals do not burn.' Is she right?
questions.a: No. Magnesium is a metal and burns with a dazzling white flame, forming white magnesium oxide, whose solution is basic and turns red litmus blue. Burning does not separate metals from non-metals; the nature of the oxide helps.
s: verdict: no
magnesium burns and is a metal
its oxide is basic, as is expected for a metal

questions.q: A student says the white powder from burning magnesium, dissolved in warm water, will turn blue litmus red. Show that this cannot happen.
questions.a: Magnesium is a metal and its oxide is basic. A basic solution turns red litmus paper blue; it cannot turn blue litmus red, which is what an acidic solution (such as sulfurous acid) does.
s: magnesium is a metal, so its oxide is basic
a basic solution turns red litmus blue
blue litmus turns red only in an acid

questions.q: Write a table of four test results for an unnamed element X that together show it is a non-metal, using appearance, hammering, the tester circuit and the litmus test on its oxide solution.
questions.a: Appearance: dull. Hammering: breaks into pieces (not malleable). Tester: bulb does not glow (poor conductor of electricity). Oxide in water: turns blue litmus red (acidic). Any consistent set of non-metal results earns the marks.
s: appearance and hammering result of a non-metal
tester result: poor conductor
oxide solution acidic: blue litmus turns red

questions.q: Four unlabelled jars hold sodium, phosphorus, magnesium ribbon and sulfur powder. With the teacher's help you may (i) place a small piece in water, (ii) burn a piece and note the flame, (iii) dissolve the burnt product in water and use litmus. Design a short plan using these to separate all four, saying what you expect to see for each.
questions.a: Water: sodium reacts vigorously with a lot of heat; the other three show no reaction. Burning: magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame and leaves white powder; its solution turns red litmus blue. Sulfur burns, gives a gas whose solution in water turns blue litmus red. Phosphorus catches fire in air and its oxide, a non-metal oxide, would be acidic. The teacher does the demonstrations in a fume hood or ventilated room.
s: water test separates sodium: vigorous reaction with heat
magnesium: dazzling white flame, white powder
magnesium solution turns red litmus blue
sulfur: gas that dissolves to turn blue litmus red
phosphorus identified by catching fire in air; safety with the teacher

questions.q: A classmate's notes read: (1) 'Sodium is kept in water because it is very reactive.' (2) 'Sulfur dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid.' (3) 'Wood and glass are non-metals.' (4) 'Oxides of non-metals are basic.' (5) 'Magnesium oxide solution turns red litmus blue.' One of the five is correct. Identify it, and correct each of the other four using the chapter.
questions.a: Line 5 is correct. (1) Sodium is kept in kerosene, because it reacts vigorously with oxygen and water. (2) Sulfur does not react with water; it is sulfur dioxide (from burning sulfur) that forms sulfurous acid in water. (3) Wood and glass are not elements, so they are neither metals nor non-metals. (4) Oxides of non-metals are acidic.
s: line 5 identified as correct
line 1 corrected: kerosene
line 2 corrected: sulfur dioxide, not sulfur
line 3 corrected: not elements
line 4 corrected: acidic

questions.q:
A teacher demonstrates three samples. Sample A burns in air with a dazzling white flame, leaving a white powder whose solution in warm water turns red litmus blue. Sample B is a dull powder that burns to give a gas; the solution of the gas turns blue litmus red; placed directly in water, B shows no reaction. Sample C is shiny, so a student calls it a metal, but its oxide in water turns blue litmus red and C does not light a tester bulb.
(a) Say whether A and B are metals or non-metals and state the rule you used.
(b) B does not react with water, yet its oxide solution is acidic. Explain.
(c) Which clue about C points to a metal and which two point to a non-metal?
(d) Decide how C should be classified for now and name one further test.
questions.a: (a) A is a metal (its oxide is basic); B is a non-metal (its oxide is acidic). Rule: oxides of metals are generally basic and those of non-metals are acidic. (b) Burning B gives an oxide that dissolves in water to form an acid; B itself does not react with water. (c) Metal: shiny. Non-metal: acidic oxide and poor conductor of electricity. (d) Treat C as a non-metal for now, since two clues outweigh one; check by hammering whether it flattens (malleability) or by another property.
s: (a) A metal, B non-metal, with the rule
(b) oxide formed on burning gives acid; B itself does not react
(c) shiny for metal; acidic oxide and poor conductor for non-metal
(d) classification as non-metal with a further test

questions.q:
A class chart has six places for 'elements'. Nine candidates are put forward: oxygen, plastic, sodium, glass, carbon, hydrogen, wood, nitrogen and paper. The chart is to be divided into a metals column and a non-metals column. The teacher wants the two columns to be as balanced as the chapter allows.
(a) Which candidates cannot be placed on the chart, and why?
(b) How many metals and how many non-metals are left among the elements?
(c) How many places remain empty?
(d) Choose one more element from the chapter to fill the empty place and justify your choice for balancing the columns.
questions.a: (a) Plastic, glass, wood and paper: they are materials, not elements, so they are neither metals nor non-metals. (b) Sodium is the only metal; oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen are four non-metals. (c) 5 elements for 6 places, so 1 place remains. (d) Add a metal from the chapter, such as magnesium, iron, copper or aluminium, to make the columns 2 and 4; the justification is that these are elements and metals by their properties.
s: (a) four materials that are not elements
(b) 1 metal and 4 non-metals
(c) one empty place
(d) a chapter metal chosen with reason to balance

questions.q: A village camp has four tasks: help patients breathe, make a well's water safe, clean a scraped knee and improve a wheat field. Which option pairs the tasks, in this order, with the non-metals the chapter names?
questions.a: Breathing needs oxygen; chlorine is used for water purification; iodine solution is the antiseptic for wounds; nitrogen is used for fertilisers and is a plant nutrient.
o: Oxygen, chlorine, iodine, nitrogen
Oxygen, iodine, chlorine, nitrogen
Nitrogen, chlorine, iodine, oxygen
Oxygen, chlorine, nitrogen, iodine

questions.q: According to the chapter's meaning of alloy, which of these is an alloy?
questions.a: Steel is a mixture of iron, a metal, and carbon, a non-metal; an alloy is a mixture of two or more metals or of a metal and a non-metal.
o: Iron mixed with carbon
Oxygen mixed with nitrogen
Pure aluminium foil
Sulfur powder stirred in water

questions.q: An eco club wants to recycle metal scrap and wants to follow what the chapter says is recycled especially in India. It has copper wire, iron rods, aluminium trays and plastic bottles. Which pair should it pick?
questions.a: The chapter says many metals, especially iron and aluminium, are recycled in India to minimise waste; plastic is not discussed.
o: Iron rods and aluminium trays
Copper wire and plastic bottles
Aluminium trays and plastic bottles
Iron rods and plastic bottles

questions.q: Four students summarise the 'Science and Society' note on alloys and special metals. Whose summary goes beyond what the chapter supports?
questions.a: The chapter also says metals and alloys are important for daily utensils and tools, so saying alloys are used only in aerospace and atomic energy is wrong.
o: Alloys are used only in aerospace and atomic energy
Alloys can be a mixture of a metal and a non-metal
Zirconium is used in atomic energy and titanium in aerospace
Alloys are important for utensils and tools used daily

questions.q: A shop assistant gives a farmer chlorine tablets for his wheat field that grows poorly. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: Chlorine is used to purify water; for plant growth the farmer needs a nitrogen fertiliser, because nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plants.
o: He needs a nitrogen fertiliser, a plant nutrient
He needs iodine solution, since it is a nutrient for plants
He should use more chlorine tablets, since chlorine feeds plants
He needs oxygen cylinders, since roots cannot breathe at all

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Our food, which gives growth and energy, depends on a non-metal.
Reason (R): Carbon is a key component of proteins, fats and carbohydrates.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: proteins, fats and carbohydrates supply growth and energy, and carbon is a key component of each.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about non-metals and alloys.
Statement 1: Chlorine is applied on wounds as an antiseptic and iodine is used to purify water.
Statement 2: Zirconium is used in atomic energy and titanium in aerospace.
Statement 3: Alloys are important only for modern technologies and not for utensils and tools.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only 2 is correct. It is the chapter's statement of the special metals. In 1 the uses are swapped (chlorine purifies water; iodine solution is an antiseptic). In 3 'only' is wrong: alloys are also important for utensils and tools.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: A scrap drive collects 120 kg of aluminium and 380 kg of iron for recycling. Iron makes up ___ percent of the metal collected.

Match each non-metal in Column I with its role in Column II.
Column I: 1. Carbon 2. Nitrogen 3. Iodine solution 4. Chlorine
Column II: a. Antiseptic applied on wounds. b. Used in water purification. c. Building block of all life forms. d. Used in making fertilisers; a plant nutrient.
Choose the correct pairing.
True or False: Alloys contain only metals. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals or of a metal and a non-metal; steel, for example, is iron (a metal) mixed with carbon (a non-metal).
s: verdict: false
correction with steel: metal with a non-metal

questions.q:
A student says, 'Chlorine and iodine are both non-metals, so a health worker can use either for the well and either for a wound.'
(a) State the use of each from the chapter.
(b) Why does the student's idea fail?
questions.a: (a) Chlorine: purifying water. Iodine solution: an antiseptic applied on wounds. (b) Each has its own use; being non-metals does not make them interchangeable.
s: (a) chlorine for water purification, iodine solution as an antiseptic
(b) the uses are specific and not interchangeable

questions.q:
(a) Name the three kinds of substances in which carbon is a key component.
(b) Explain why this makes carbon essential for both a growing child and a farmer's plants.
questions.a: (a) Proteins, fats and carbohydrates. (b) They are necessary for growth and energy in living things, and carbon is the building block of all life forms, plants included.
s: (a) proteins, fats and carbohydrates
(b) they provide growth and energy; carbon is in all life forms

questions.q:
A colony keeps separate bins for old iron and aluminium items and pays ₹2,000 a month to run them without earning any cash.
(a) State the benefit the chapter gives for recycling these metals.
(b) Is the project pointless? Explain.
questions.a: (a) It minimises waste and contributes to sustainability. (b) No: the chapter's benefit is less waste and sustainability, not only money, so the project has value even without cash income.
s: (a) minimises waste and contributes to sustainability
(b) not pointless: the benefit is not only cash

questions.q: A student reads that titanium is used in aerospace and zirconium in atomic energy and writes, 'So only rare special metals matter in industry; common iron and aluminium do not.' Correct her using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter says metals and their alloys are important for daily use as utensils and tools, and are essential in almost every industry; it also says iron and aluminium are recycled in India, so they matter a great deal.
s: metals and alloys matter for utensils, tools and almost every industry
iron and aluminium are named as widely recycled, so important

questions.q: Maya says, 'Only iron and aluminium are recycled in India.' Is she right?
questions.a: Partly. The chapter says iron and aluminium are recycled, but it says many metals are recycled, 'especially' iron and aluminium, so 'only' goes beyond what the chapter says.
s: verdict: partly right
iron and aluminium are named as recycled
'many metals ... especially' means 'only' is too strong

questions.q: A shopkeeper labels a steel almirah as 'pure iron, an element'. Show why this cannot be correct, using the chapter's meaning of alloy and element.
questions.a: Steel is a mixture of iron and carbon, so it is an alloy, not a pure metal. An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances; steel contains two different elements mixed together.
s: steel is a mixture of iron and carbon, an alloy
an element cannot be broken into simpler substances
steel holds two elements, so it is not one

questions.q: Describe a small rural clinic's day in which at least two non-metals and one metal or alloy are each needed for a different job. Name each and say what it does.
questions.a: Example: oxygen helps a patient breathe; iodine solution is applied on a wound as an antiseptic; chlorine purifies the clinic's drinking water; and steel instruments or aluminium utensils are used for daily work. Any valid situation with two non-metals and one metal or alloy, each with a correct job.
s: two non-metals named with correct jobs
a metal or alloy named with a correct job
the situation is realistic and consistent

questions.q: A school magazine page is titled 'Do we really need non-metals?' List the role in daily life of oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, chlorine and iodine. Then correct two captions printed on the page: 'Steel is a pure metal' and 'Non-metals have no uses'.
questions.a: Oxygen: breathing. Carbon: building block of life, in proteins, fats and carbohydrates. Nitrogen: used in fertilisers, a plant nutrient. Chlorine: water purification. Iodine solution: antiseptic on wounds. Steel is an alloy: a mixture of iron (a metal) and carbon (a non-metal). Non-metals matter greatly for survival, health and growth.
s: oxygen and carbon roles
nitrogen role
chlorine and iodine roles
steel corrected: alloy of iron and carbon
non-metals have important uses, with an example

questions.q: A class debates, 'Metals are more important than non-metals.' Give two facts from the chapter for the motion and two against it, then give your own judgement in one sentence supported by those facts.
questions.a: For: metals are strong and lustrous, conduct heat and electricity (pans, wires); alloys such as steel ropes hold heavy loads. Against: oxygen is needed to breathe; carbon builds life forms; nitrogen helps plants grow; chlorine and iodine protect health. Judgement: each is needed for different jobs, so neither group can be called more important in general. Any reasoned judgement that uses the facts earns the mark.
s: a first fact supporting metals
a second fact supporting metals
a first fact supporting non-metals
a second fact supporting non-metals
a judgement that uses the facts

questions.q:
A school eco club in Jaipur has collected 30 kg of aluminium trays, 140 kg of iron rods, 12 kg of copper wire and 90 kg of plastic bottles. The dealer's van can carry only two kinds of items, with a total of at most 200 kg. The dealer offers ₹30 per kg for iron, ₹110 per kg for aluminium and ₹600 per kg for copper. The club wants to minimise waste, and also needs money for a science fair.
(a) Which of the four items are metals, and which is neither a metal nor a non-metal element?
(b) Which pairs of items fit in the van?
(c) Work out the money earned and the mass recycled for iron with aluminium, and for iron with copper.
(d) Choose one pair and justify the choice using the chapter and your numbers.
questions.a: (a) Aluminium, iron and copper are metals; plastic is a material, not an element. (b) Iron + aluminium = 170 kg and iron + copper = 152 kg fit; iron + plastic = 230 kg does not. (c) Iron + aluminium: 140 x 30 + 30 x 110 = ₹7,500 for 170 kg. Iron + copper: 140 x 30 + 12 x 600 = ₹11,400 for 152 kg. (d) Either can be defended: iron with aluminium recycles more mass and matches the metals the chapter highlights for reducing waste; iron with copper earns ₹3,900 more for the fair. A reasoned choice earns the mark.
s: (a) three metals; plastic is not an element
(b) fitting pairs identified
(c) ₹7,500 for 170 kg and ₹11,400 for 152 kg
(d) reasoned choice between waste and money

questions.q:
A village health camp has a budget of ₹4,500. It must make a well's water safe, treat a boy's scraped knee, and help a farmer whose wheat grows poorly. The camp can buy chlorine for ₹1,800, iodine solution for ₹900 and a nitrogen fertiliser for ₹2,600.
(a) Which item serves which of the three needs?
(b) What do the three cost together, and by how much do they exceed the budget?
(c) Which pairs of items fit within the budget, and how much is left in each case?
(d) Choose which need the camp will leave unmet, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Chlorine for water, iodine solution for the wound (antiseptic), nitrogen fertiliser for the wheat. (b) ₹1,800 + ₹900 + ₹2,600 = ₹5,300, which is ₹800 over. (c) Chlorine + iodine = ₹2,700 (₹1,800 left); chlorine + fertiliser = ₹4,400 (₹100 left); iodine + fertiliser = ₹3,500 (₹1,000 left). (d) Any reasoned choice: leaving out the fertiliser keeps both health needs and ₹1,800 spare; leaving out iodine is the cheapest wound-care saving but leaves the knee without an antiseptic.
s: (a) chlorine, iodine and nitrogen matched to needs
(b) ₹5,300 and ₹800 over
(c) three pairs with money left
(d) reasoned choice of the need left unmet
